```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
inla_available <- bdlnm::check_inla()
```

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(bdlnm)
library(dlnm)
library(splines)
library(utils)
```

In this vignette, we will explain how to perform a B-DLNM for a multi-location study, using an IID random effect model in function of each city. Explain difference from the two-staged classic frequentist approach.

# italy dataset

As an example for this vignette, we will use the built-in dataset `italy` which contains daily temperature and mortality data in 87 Italian cities between 1 January 2011 and 31 December 2021.

```{r}
head(italy)
```

Using Bayesian Distributed Non-Linear Models (B-DLNM) we will estimate the lagged effect of the temperature exposure to mortality in all the population, taking 21 days of lags, specific for each of the 87 Italian cities and the combined effect for all Italy.

# Set DLNM parameters

We will start by building the global crossbasis for all Italy with the `dlnm` package. Because the long dataset contains one temperature series for each city, we use the `group` argument to identify the city-specific consecutive time series. This prevents lagged values from carrying over from one age group to the other.

We will use a natural spline with three knots for the exposure–response function, placed at the 10th, 75th, and 90th percentiles of daily mean temperature, and a natural spline for the lag–response function, with knots equally spaced on the log scale up to a maximum lag of 21 days:

```{r}
# Exposure-response and lag-response spline parameters
dlnm_var <- list(
  var_prc = c(10, 75, 90),
  var_fun = "ns",
  lag_fun = "ns",
  max_lag = 21,
  lagnk = 3
)


# Cross-basis parameters
argvar <- list(
  fun = dlnm_var$var_fun,
  knots = quantile(italy$tmean, dlnm_var$var_prc / 100, na.rm = TRUE),
  Bound = range(italy$tmean, na.rm = TRUE)
)

arglag <- list(
  fun = dlnm_var$lag_fun,
  knots = logknots(dlnm_var$max_lag, nk = dlnm_var$lagnk)
)

# Create crossbasis
cb <- crossbasis(italy$tmean, lag = dlnm_var$max_lag, argvar, arglag, group = italy$city_name)
```

Let’s define the seasonality of the mortality time series using a natural spline with 8 degrees of freedom per year, which flexibly controls for long-term and seasonal trends in mortality:

```{r}
# Seasonality of mortality time series
seas <- ns(italy$date, df = round(8 * length(unique(italy$date)) / 365.25))
```

Let's calculate the day of the week which we will use to control for the weekly seasonality:

```{r}
italy$dow <- lubridate::wday(
  italy$date,
  label = TRUE,
  abbr = TRUE,
  week_start = 1,
  locale = "C"
)
```

Finally, we also define the temperature values for which predictions will be generated. These correspond to an evenly spaced grid with a 0.1ºC step covering the full range of observed temperatures in the data:

```{r}
# Prediction values (equidistant points)
temp <- round(seq(min(italy$tmean), max(italy$tmean), by = 0.1), 1)
# Ensure it falls inside the range of temperatures after rounding:
temp <- temp[temp >= min(italy$tmean) & temp <= max(italy$tmean)]
```

# Fit the model and posterior samples

Fit the Bayesian DLNM using the function `bdlnm()`. In this example, we specify a Poisson model including the cross-basis term, a seasonal component, and an indicator for the day of the week. We draw 1000 samples from the posterior distribution and set a seed for reproducibility.

We will change the INLA approximation method to "adaptive" which uses the usual simplified Laplace approximation for fixed effects and small random-effect components and uses the faster Gaussian approximation for larger random-effects components:

```{r, eval = inla_available}
italy$id_city <- as.numeric(factor(italy$city_code))
mod <- bdlnm(
  deaths ~ cb + f(id_city, cb, model = "iid") + dow + seas,
  data = italy,
  family = "poisson",
  sample.arg = list(n = 1000, seed = 5243),
  control.inla = list(strategy = "adaptive")
)
```

The returned object is of class bdlnm and contains the fitted INLA model, the crossbasis objects included in the formula, and posterior samples of the estimated coefficients together with their summaries (mean, standard deviation, median, and lower and upper credible-interval bounds).

```{r, eval = inla_available}
str(mod, max.level = 1)
```

# Uncentered predicted effects

We first predict the uncentered exposure–lag–response association over the candidate temperature grid, for the global and for each of the cities:

```{r, eval = inla_available}
cpred_uncentered <- bcrosspred(mod, combine_effects = ~ cb + f(id_city, cb, model = "iid"), exp_at = temp, cen = FALSE)
```

A `bcrosspred` object is returned containing posterior samples of the estimated exposure–lag–response association for the supplied temperature values and lags, together with their summaries.

```{r, eval = inla_available}
str(cpred_uncentered)
```

# Optimal exposure value

An optimal exposure value can be estimated from the predicted overall effects and subsequently used to center the predictions. For example, in a temperature-mortality study like this, we can estimate the minimum mortality temperature (MMT), defined as the temperature at which the predicted overall mortality risk is minimized for each posterior sample.

```{r, eval = inla_available}
mmt <- optimal_exposure(cpred_uncentered)

str(mmt)
```

We can visualize the posterior distribution of the MMT estimates. It is useful to inspect this distribution to assess whether multiple candidate optimal exposure values exist and to verify that the median provides a reasonable centering value:

```{r fig.width = 7, eval = inla_available}
plot(
  mmt,
  xlab = "Temperature (ºC)",
  main = paste0("MMT (Median = ", round(mmt$summary[["0.5quant"]], 1), "ºC)")
)
```

For this example, we use the median of the posterior MMT distribution as the centering value.

```{r, eval = inla_available}
cen <- mmt$summary[["0.5quant"]]
cen
```

# Centered predicted effects

We recalculate the exposure–lag–response association over the supplied temperature grid, this time centering the predictions at the selected MMT value:

```{r, eval = inla_available}
cpred <- bcrosspred(mod, exp_at = temp, cen = cen)
```

For instance, the estimated `crossbasis` coefficients are stored as:

```{r, eval = inla_available}
cpred$coefficients |>
  head(c(5, 5))
```

The relative risks (RR) for each temperature–lag combination are also stored in an array for each posterior sample. For example, for the first sample:

```{r, eval = inla_available}
cpred$matRRfit[,, "sample1"] |>
  head()
```

The overall cumulative effects for each temperature (summing across all lags) are stored in:

```{r, eval = inla_available}
cpred$allRRfit |>
  head(c(5, 5))
```

Summaries of these effects across posterior samples are also available:

```{r, eval = inla_available}
cpred$matRRfit.summary |>
  head(5)

cpred$allRRfit.summary |>
  head(5)
```

# Plot

Several visualizations can be produced from these predictions using the `plot()` method.

For example, we can plot the overall cumulative effect for each temperature value (suming across all lags):

```{r fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, eval = inla_available}
plot(
  cpred,
  "overall",
  xlab = "Temperature (ºC)",
  ylab = "Relative Risk",
  col = 4,
  main = "Overall",
  log = "y"
)
```

Alternatively, we can display the posterior sampling variability by plotting the curves from all posterior samples instead of the credible interval:

```{r fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4, eval = inla_available}
plot(
  cpred,
  "overall",
  xlab = "Temperature (ºC)",
  ylab = "Relative Risk",
  col = 4,
  main = "Overall",
  log = "y",
  ci = "sampling"
)
```

We can also visualize the full exposure–lag–response association using a 3-D surface:

```{r fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6, eval = inla_available}
plot(
  cpred,
  "3d",
  zlab = "Relative risk",
  col = 4,
  lphi = 60,
  cex.axis = 0.6,
  xlab = "Temperature (ºC)",
  main = "3D graph of temperature effect"
)
```

A contour plot provides a 2-D projection of the same relationship:

```{r fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6, eval = inla_available}
plot(
  cpred,
  "contour",
  xlab = "Temperature (ºC)",
  ylab = "Lag",
  main = "Contour plot"
)
```

We can also examine the lag–response association for a high temperature (e.g., the 99th percentile):

```{r fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6, eval = inla_available}
htemp <- round(quantile(london$tmean, 0.99), 1)
plot(
  cpred,
  "slices",
  ci = "bars",
  type = "p",
  pch = 19,
  exp_at = htemp,
  ylab = "RR",
  main = paste0("Association for a high temperature (", htemp, "ºC)")
)
```

Or the exposure–response association at lag 0:

```{r fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6, eval = inla_available}
plot(
  cpred,
  "slices",
  lag_at = 0,
  col = 4,
  ylab = "RR",
  main = paste0("Association at lag 0")
)
```
